items.title: Schuller Gunther — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Morgenstern – Dan did, and the great Hollywood film composer, Quincy Jones. Quincy Jones got it. So I’m in very honored company.

ctx.x: Can you just converse a little bit about the NEA Jazz Master award that you were a recipient of.

Yeah, sure. The first I have to say about getting a Jazz Master award: I was totally stunned to be told that I was going to get this award, and by the way, just incidentally, that there was a nice little financial award included in that. But for me, with all that I’ve said about my involvement in jazz, I consider my role to have finally only a peripheral role and a very minor role, although in some ways, important or influential. I’m not Charlie Parker. I’m no Dizzy Gillespie. I’m no Duke Ellington or anything like

that. I’m just someone who helped in a certain way. So for me to get the Jazz Master award, particularly when it has gone almost entirely – and should go – to performers or players and composers, if there are composers. There aren’t that many composers. Most jazz players are improvisers, which is a form of composing, of course. But it isn’t composing like Ellington did. Now they have this new category, Jazz Masters, and the attached word is advocates, and I certainly have been that. So I’m very proud to have…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: And Gunther Schuller and Martin Williams had a program called “The Scope of Jazz.”

ctx.x: It helped inform their choices of what to play, yeah, sure. It made them sound more informed.

And actually, one of the reasons why I did that, although I didn’t start initially, was that I’ve done quite a lot of radio over time. I started out at WBAI in New York. And Gunther Schuller and Martin Williams had a program called “The Scope of Jazz.” And Martin had to bow out and he turned it over to me. And so, that was back in the sixties. Nat Hentoff was also in it. Gunther was the first one and then he moved to Boston. Anyway, it was

like a series, one hour jazz, a Sunday night broadcast. But then once I got with the Institute we started, when WBGO was the new jazz radio station in Newark back thirty- some years ago, they came to us at the Institute and asked us to do a weekly program, and we decided to call it “Jazz from the Archives.” And so Ed Berger and Vincent Pelote and I and some of the other people who worked for us would take turns doing the program. We started out, the station didn’t have very much. They had no record library. We of…
